plain: Amendment 82 would add to Colorado’s constitution a right to buy natural gas for cooking or heating, and a right for utilities to sell it. Buying and selling gas is already legal today.

short_version.text: Gas is legal and for sale today, and no Colorado elected body has banned gas stoves or heaters in homes. Amendment 82 would make buying and selling gas a constitutional right, which could block future state and local limits, such as rules steering new buildings to electric heat. Burning gas in buildings adds to Colorado's climate pollution. Whether switching saves a household money depends on the home, and the main bill comparison comes from the gas industry.

agree_means: Agreeing writes a right to buy and sell natural gas for homes and businesses into the constitution. That could limit state or local rules that restrict gas.
disagree_means: Disagreeing keeps current law. Gas stays legal and for sale, and the state and cities keep their power to write or change gas rules.

stakes.text: The gas industry's trade group says electricity costs 4.3 times as much as gas per unit of energy in Colorado, and that a new gas-heated home could save $614 to $1,065 a year compared with a heat pump. A federal lab found heat pumps cut bills for homes now heated by electricity, oil or propane. Supporters of Amendment 82 say switching would cost a household $1,100 a year; this guide found no study behind that figure.

research_notes: Method: Claude in Chrome was not connected, so pages that blocked plain fetches or only render in JavaScript were read in the built-in browser in my own tab. Browser reads (marked via: browser): EIA Colorado state analysis (eia.gov/states/CO/analysis), Inside Climate News (Jul 2026), CPR News (Dec 2022 cold snap) and the original Colorado Newsline article (the syndicated copy sits behind a Cloudflare check) were read in the browser because plain fetches failed; their quotes were copied from the rendered page. Colorado state sites (puc.colorado.gov, energyoffice.colorado.gov) and the National Laboratory of the Rockies press release return 403 to clients without a browser user agent, so I also confirmed each of those quotes in the browser and marked them via: browser. All other pages were fetched directly and every quote was checked against the fetched text (whitespace-normalized). The shared web-search budget ran out mid-task, so some gaps below could not be closed. Length: about 850 words of text, above the 300-500 target, because the request asked for depth on this statement. Not found: (1) The 2025 CDPHE greenhouse gas inventory (Jan 2026) sector shares: the documents sit in a JavaScript viewer I could not read, so the emissions figures are older and defined differently: 23 percent is 2020, Legislative Council staff, gas burned in homes, businesses AND industry; 8 percent is 2015, homes and businesses only (Colorado Newsline, 2021). (2) Any figure for the share of outdoor air pollution (NOx, ozone) from burning gas in buildings, and a CDPHE source on the 2026 furnace and water heater NOx limits. (3) A Colorado installed price for heat pumps from a non-seller source (EnergySage and contractor pages were excluded as sellers). (4) A count of gas-utility jobs: the federal USEER figure for Fuels covers all fuels. (5) Any study behind the campaign claim of $1,100 a year; it is reported as a supporter claim only. Double-check: (a) Denver code: Colorado Politics (Feb 2025) says Denver banned gas furnaces and water heaters in new commercial and multifamily buildings, while the Denver Post (Oct 2026) says gas appliances are not prohibited in Denver. I stayed with the Blue Book and Denver Post wording and did not state Denver's rules. (b) The 600,000-customer figure is the Colorado Energy Office and CDPHE testimony as reported by the Denver Gazette; the PUC fact sheet says recovered methane and other options also count, so electrification is not the only route. (c) The gas trade group (AGA) cost analysis covers new single-family homes and is an industry document; the NREL release is national. (d) The Blue Book fiscal note and the 2026 Legislative Council fiscal statement say local governments with gas-limiting codes may need to change them. (e) EIA's 2020 household survey (RECS) shows Colorado with 2.26 million homes, 83 percent using gas for some purpose and 10 percent all-electric. I did not quote it because PDF table rows extract unreliably. (f) Where a page has no publication date the date is the access date with date_basis accessed. (g) The Blue Book argument for and against are a single paragraph each; the Blue Book is quoted for them as required. (h) The Inside Climate News article has at least one error (it says the PUC set the 41 percent rule in 2022; the PUC decision is Dec 1, 2025), so I used it only for the legal expert's comments, the no-caveats observation and not for its other claims. Editor, 2026-10-16: the bill comparison is now attributed to the American Gas Association in the sentence itself, and the campaign's $1,100 figure is marked as unsupported by any study found.
